items.question: How is password entropy measured?
items.answer: Entropy is calculated as Length × log2(Pool Size). A 20-character password spanning all 94 ASCII characters provides over 131 bits of generation entropy, rendering brute-force attacks mathematically impossible.

items.question: Why choose a multi-word passphrase over random characters?
items.answer: Passphrases combine high entropy with human memorability. A 5-word passphrase drawn from a standard dictionary offers over 64 bits of entropy while remaining easy to type without transcription errors.

items.question: How is cryptographically secure randomness guaranteed?
items.answer: Randomness is sourced exclusively from the browser crypto.getRandomValues API with rejection sampling to eliminate modulo bias. Math.random is strictly forbidden.

items.question: Are generated passwords saved or logged in any way?
items.answer: Never. Passwords exist only in active browser memory and disappear when the page is refreshed. Nothing is ever sent to a server.

items.question: What does the ambiguous character exclusion option do?
items.answer: Excluding ambiguous characters removes visually confusing glyphs such as uppercase I, lowercase l, numeral 1, uppercase O, and numeral 0 to prevent transcription mistakes.

items.question: Does every generated password include characters from every selected set?
items.answer: Yes. The algorithm guarantees that at least one character from each selected class (uppercase, lowercase, number, symbol) is present, shuffled randomly via Fisher-Yates.

items.question: What dictionary powers the passphrase generator?
items.answer: Passphrases utilize curated wordlists inspired by the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) large wordlist, ensuring words are distinct, easy to spell, and free from offensive terms.

items.question: How long would it take a supercomputer to crack a 100-bit password?
items.answer: Cracking a 100-bit password would require testing 2^100 combinations, a computational task that would take billions of years using all combined supercomputers on Earth.
